issues.legal_issue: Earlier judgments do not bar a claim that a mosque is a public wakf when the mosque’s public character was not raised and decided in those proceedings.
material_facts: The earlier suits concerned religious ceremonies, the right to appoint or act as Imam, and management of the mosque.
The public character of the mosque was not in issue in those suits; some statements about ownership or control were made in proceedings directed to other questions or were obiter.
The present suit sought relief concerning the mosque as a public trust.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgments did not operate as res judicata against the claim that the mosque was a public wakf.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, res judicata requires, among other things, identity of the subject matter and a final decision on the matter in issue by a competent court. The Court examined the earlier pleadings and judgments and held that the public character of the mosque had not been decided; findings made in cases about management or religious functions did not determine that issue.

predicates.public_wakf_claim: The proceeding seeks a determination that a religious property is a public wakf.
predicates.earlier_litigation: The parties rely on judgments from earlier litigation between them.
predicates.public_character_not_decided: The earlier proceedings addressed other rights or management questions without finally deciding whether the property was a public wakf.

issues.definition: When a public-wakf claim follows earlier litigation that did not decide the property’s public character, the earlier judgments do not bar that claim.

issues.legal_issue: A mosque is a public wakf when the founder’s intention to dedicate it, divestment of ownership, and public access for worship are established, and religious adjuncts used for worship form part of the mosque.
material_facts: The village had no mosque, and members of the Muslim community obtained permission from the landowner to construct one.
A written agreement described the building as a mosque for worship, provided for separate entrances, and recorded that the builders would claim only the right to worship and maintain it.
The owner consented to the agreement, the mosque was built, and the Muslim public was allowed to worship there over a long period.
A platform, rooms, a water facility, a latrine, a minaret, and other facilities were used for prayers and related religious purposes.
issues.conclusion: The mosque was permanently and irrevocably dedicated as a public wakf, and its religious adjuncts formed part of the same wakf unit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hanafi Mahomedan law, no prescribed form of declaration is needed; intention to dedicate may be inferred from conduct. Dedication is complete when the founder divests ownership and permits public prayers; in the case of a mosque, permission to worship may constitute delivery of possession. A separate public entrance is also a relevant requirement. Additions used for prayer or related religious purposes are accretions to the mosque. The Court relied on Jewan Doss Sahoo v. Shah Kubeer-ood-Deen, Adam Sheik v. Isha Sheik, Saiyad Maher Husein v. Haji Alimahomed, Akbarally v. Mahomedally, Miru v. Ramgopal, Abdul Rahim Khan v. Fakir Mohammad Shah, Masjid Shahid Ganj Mosque v. Shromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, Musaheb Khan v. Raj Kummar Bakshi, Maula Baksh v. Amiruddin, and Mohammad Shah v. Fazihuddin Ansari.

rule.if: public_mosque_wakf_claim and founder_intended_dedication and ownership_divested and public_worship_permitted and separate_public_entrance and adjuncts_used_for_religious_purposes

predicates.public_mosque_wakf_claim: The proceeding seeks recognition of a mosque and associated facilities as a public religious endowment.
predicates.founder_intended_dedication: The owner’s words or conduct show an intention to dedicate the property as a mosque for public worship.
predicates.ownership_divested: The owner relinquished ownership of the mosque property, including by permitting the public to use it for worship.
predicates.public_worship_permitted: Members of the public were allowed to offer prayers in the mosque.
predicates.separate_public_entrance: The mosque had a distinct entrance available for public access.
predicates.adjuncts_used_for_religious_purposes: Associated structures or facilities were used for prayers or purposes incidental to religious worship.

issues.definition: When a public-mosque claim establishes the founder’s dedication, divestment, public worship, and a separate entrance, religiously used adjuncts are included in the public wakf.

issues.legal_issue: Earlier final judgments bar a renewed claim that a burial ground is private when they decided that the same burial ground was public.
material_facts: Earlier litigation repeatedly concerned whether the burial ground was private or public and whether shops could be built on it.
Courts held that the burial ground was public and directed removal of shops; later attempts to avoid or set aside those decisions failed.
The present dispute again concerned the public or private character of the same burial ground.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgments operated as res judicata on the public character of the burial ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars relitigation where the parties and subject matter are the same, the matter was finally decided, and the earlier decision was made by a court of competent jurisdiction. The Court relied on the prior judgments concerning the burial ground, including the proceedings arising from O.S. No. 331 of 1915 and the subsequent unsuccessful suits to avoid its effect.

predicates.public_burial_ground_claim: The proceeding disputes whether a burial ground is public or private.
predicates.same_burial_ground: The current dispute concerns the same burial ground addressed in the earlier proceedings.
predicates.prior_final_public_status_decision: A competent court previously and finally decided that the burial ground was public, and attempts to overturn or evade that decision failed.

issues.definition: A renewed dispute over a burial ground’s status is barred when a competent court has already finally decided the public status of that same ground.

issues.legal_issue: A burial ground is a public wakf when public use for burials is established by longstanding or repeated use, and a private family burial ground loses that character when members of the public are permitted to bury their dead there.
material_facts: Muslims from the village had buried their dead in the disputed ground over a long period, and the defendants did not deny that public use.

The defendants charged pit fees and other incidental charges, but the burial ground was treated as public in earlier judgments and was registered as a burial ground after an application by members of the defendants’ family.
There was no evidence distinguishing the two parts of the burial ground or showing that either part was reserved for the family alone.
issues.conclusion: Both parts of the burial ground constituted a public graveyard and public wakf; the community could bury its dead there subject to applicable charges.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mahomedan law, a public graveyard may be established by immemorial user even without direct proof of dedication. Repeated burials by members of the community support a presumption of public dedication; a family graveyard is confined to the founder and family, and public burials change its character. An entry describing land as a public graveyard in revenue or historical records is conclusive proof of its public character. The Court relied on Ballabh Das v. Nur Mohammad, Imam Baksh v. Mandar Narsingh Puri, Sheorai Chamar v. Mudeer Khan, Qadir Baksh v. Saddullah, and Mohammad Kassam v. Abdul Gafoor.

predicates.public_burial_ground_claim: The proceeding seeks recognition of a burial ground as public rather than private.
predicates.repeated_public_burials: Members of the wider religious community repeatedly buried their dead in the ground over a substantial period.
predicates.no_family_only_restriction: The ground was not confined to the founder and family, and no evidence established a distinction reserving any part for family use alone.

issues.definition: A burial ground used repeatedly by the public, without a restriction confining it to one family, is a public wakf.

issues.legal_issue: The consent requirement for bringing a suit concerning a wakf does not bar the suit when the relevant board has not been constituted and cannot give consent.
material_facts: The suit sought relief concerning public wakf properties.
No board contemplated by the governing legislation had been constituted when the suit was brought.
issues.conclusion: The absence of written consent from the board did not make the suit unmaintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 55(2) of the Muslim Wakfs Act, 1954 required the Board’s written consent for specified suits concerning wakfs. The requirement could not apply when no Board had been constituted and the consent mechanism was incapable of operation.

predicates.wakf_relief_suit: The proceeding seeks relief relating to the administration or protection of a wakf.
predicates.board_not_constituted: The statutory board whose consent is required had not been established when the suit was filed.

issues.definition: A suit seeking relief concerning a wakf is not barred for want of board consent when the board had not been constituted.

issues.legal_issue: A suit to administer a public religious trust and address its mismanagement may proceed against persons acting as de facto managers even if they deny being trustees or assert personal ownership.
material_facts: The defendants managed the properties and enjoyed their usufruct, although they asserted that the properties belonged to them.

The properties were found to be public wakfs, and the defendants had allowed the mosque to fall into disrepair, failed to maintain the burial ground, built shops on part of the graveyard, and disobeyed decrees requiring their removal.
The plaintiffs sought removal of the managers and a scheme for administering the public trust properties.
issues.conclusion: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applied, and the evidence established a case for framing a scheme for the mosque, its adjuncts, and the burial ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies where there is an alleged breach of an express or constructive trust created for a public, charitable, or religious purpose, or where the Court’s directions are necessary for its administration. De facto managers who manage trust property and enjoy its benefits may be trustees de son tort; their assertion of personal title does not make them mere trespassers. The Court approved Mahomed Shirazi v. Province of Bengal and Ramdas Bhagat v. Krishna Prasad, and also relied on Abdul Rahim Khan v. Fakir Mohammad Shah.

rule.if: public_trust_administration_suit and defendants_act_as_managers and public_trust_mismanagement and court_directions_needed

predicates.public_trust_administration_suit: The proceeding seeks directions for administration of a public religious or charitable trust.
predicates.defendants_act_as_managers: The defendants in fact managed the trust property or enjoyed its benefits.
predicates.public_trust_mismanagement: The managers neglected the property, misused it, or failed to comply with orders protecting it.
predicates.court_directions_needed: The administration of the public trust requires directions from the court.

issues.definition: A court may frame an administration scheme when a public-trust suit shows that de facto managers mismanaged trust property and judicial directions are needed.

issues.legal_issue: The right to officiate as Imam in a public mosque is not hereditary in the absence of an established custom or usage, and a candidate must be suitable to lead prayers.
material_facts: Members of the defendants’ family had acted as Imams, but not continuously.
There was no clear evidence of a custom or usage making the office hereditary.
The mosque was a public mosque, and the Court said selection of an Imam was normally for the Muslim community, subject to the Imam’s required qualities and knowledge.
issues.conclusion: No hereditary right to officiate as Imam was established; the community could select an Imam according to Muslim law and usage, and the Court could consider a suitable member of the defendants’ family when framing the scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mahomedan law, hereditary succession to the office of Imam is not favoured without a contrary custom or usage. An Imam must possess the requisite virtues and religious knowledge. The Court also observed that the Muslim community normally chooses the Imam and that the welfare of the wakf must guide any administrative arrangement.

predicates.public_mosque_imam_dispute: The proceeding concerns who may lead prayers in a public mosque.
predicates.no_proven_hereditary_custom: No established custom or usage shows that the office of Imam passes by inheritance.

issues.definition: In a dispute over leadership of prayers in a public mosque, the office is not hereditary when no contrary custom or usage is proved.

issues.legal_issue: A religious site remains private when the evidence does not establish its dedication as a public wakf.
material_facts: The courts below found that the Dargah was the private property of the defendants and that there was no evidence that it had been constituted as a public wakf.
The respondents did not press their appeal challenging the decision concerning the Dargah.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the Dargah was private property remained undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court left undisturbed the concurrent finding that the Dargah had not been proved to be a public wakf, particularly after the challenge to that finding was not pressed.

predicates.appeal_challenges_private_site_finding: An appeal seeks to overturn a finding that a religious site is private property.
predicates.no_evidence_of_public_dedication: The record contains no evidence establishing that the site was dedicated as a public religious trust.
predicates.challenge_not_pressed: The party challenging the finding does not pursue that challenge.

issues.definition: When no public dedication is proved and the challenge to a private-property finding is not pursued, that finding remains undisturbed.
